theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is emotional intelligence (EI)?
options: A high score on a test of reasoning and memory
The ability to recognise and manage emotions
A habit of hiding all feelings while at work
Technical knowledge of the public service rules

questions.stem: Which of these is one of the main parts of emotional intelligence in Goleman's model?
options: Strategic planning
Technical expertise
Financial control
Self-regulation

questions.stem: Dionne Henry, a supervisor at a tax office in Spanish Town, notices that she becomes short-tempered with staff late on Fridays. Which EI skill is she using when she notices this?

Social skill
Self-awareness
Inner motivation

questions.stem: What is an emotional "trigger"?

A rule that bans emotions at work
A tool for measuring staff performance
A meeting held to settle a grievance

questions.stem: At a municipal corporation meeting, a councillor criticises Andre's report in front of everyone. Andre feels angry. What is the most emotionally intelligent first response?

questions.stem: Which method gives a manager the most balanced view of how her emotions and behaviour affect others?

Reading a magazine quiz about feelings

To prove to others that she is always right

questions.stem: What does empathy mean in the workplace?

Agreeing with whatever others want
Feeling sorry for staff who make errors
Keeping your own feelings to yourself

questions.stem: A usually cheerful clerk in a public hospital's records office has been quiet, avoiding eye contact and eating lunch alone for a week. What should her supervisor do?
options: Ignore it, as personal matters are private
Talk with her privately and ask how she is

Warn her that her attitude must improve

questions.stem: Which behaviour best shows active listening?
options: Planning your reply while the other person speaks
Checking your phone to save time
Finishing the speaker's sentences for them
Summarising what you heard and checking it

questions.stem: Which is a healthy way for a manager to handle her own stress during a busy budget period at a ministry?

Taking it out on her team in meetings
Planning priorities and taking short breaks
Keeping all her worries completely bottled up

questions.stem: In emotional intelligence, what does self-motivation mainly involve?

Working only when a bonus is offered

questions.stem: A team's proposal for a new community programme is turned down by the agency's board. Which response shows resilience?
options: Blaming the board publicly for the result
Learning from the feedback and trying again

questions.stem: Why does emotional intelligence matter for a manager in a public body?
options: It removes the need to follow procedures
It means the manager never feels upset

questions.stem: Two officers at a municipal office argue loudly over a shared task. As their manager, what should you do first?
options: Take the side of the more senior officer
Tell them both to stop being childish
Calm things, then hear each one privately

questions.stem: Why can naming an emotion to yourself ("I feel frustrated") help you to manage it?
options: It helps you think before reacting
It makes the feeling disappear for good
It shows others you are always in control

questions.stem: Karen must tell a long-serving officer that his reports contain repeated errors. Which approach shows the most emotional intelligence?
options: Email the criticism so she avoids a hard talk
Speak privately, give facts and listen to him

questions.stem: A director tells Marcia that her presentation was poorly organised. What is the most emotionally intelligent response?
options: Argue that the director misunderstood it
Say nothing and complain to colleagues later

questions.stem: A team in a Kingston ministry includes staff from several countries in the region. Why should the manager consider cultural differences in how emotions are shown?
options: So she can treat some cultures as more emotional
So she can avoid working with some staff

options: Her mood is likely to spread to the team
The team will become more cheerful to balance it

options: Tell her everyone feels that way sometimes
Listen and help her reach professional support

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an employee assistance programme (EAP)?
options: To check staff attendance and lateness
To give staff extra paid holidays

questions.stem: A new manager joins a municipal corporation office where staff distrust management. Which first step best builds relationships?
options: Announce many changes in her first week
Spend most of her time in her own office

questions.stem: Which behaviour most helps a manager build trust with a frontline team?
options: Showing genuine interest in their work
Using humour at one person's expense

questions.stem: What is the difference between managing an emotion and suppressing it?
options: Managing means never showing any feelings
Managing means choosing how to express it

questions.stem: Late at night, a manager receives an unfair email from another department and writes an angry reply. What should she do?
options: Send it at once so the matter is settled

questions.stem: Which practice best helps a team develop emotional intelligence together?
options: Banning any discussion of feelings at work

questions.stem: A team leader often loses his temper with members of the public at a service counter. How can his manager best help him develop?

questions.stem: An upset man shouts at a clerk at a passport office because of a long wait. What should the clerk do first?
options: Shout back to show she will not be bullied

questions.stem: How can emotions affect a manager's decisions?
options: They have no effect if the manager is senior
They always improve the quality of decisions

questions.stem: Why should a manager know her own emotional strengths and limits?
options: So she can avoid ever feeling stress
So she can blame her limits on others
So she can plan and seek support
So she can avoid all difficult tasks

questions.stem: A manager scores highly on an online EI self-test. How should she treat the result?
options: As one view, checked against others' feedback
As proof that she needs no further development
As a reason to stop asking staff for feedback
As a score to share with the whole department

questions.stem: A ministry is merging two departments, and staff are anxious about their jobs. What should the manager do?
options: Tell staff not to worry and change the subject
Share what she can and hear concerns

questions.stem: Which is the most effective way to recognise an officer's good work?
options: General praise for the whole team once a year
Praise given only when a director is present

questions.stem: A manager wants to show empathy to her staff. Which action respects their privacy?
options: Asking staff to share their family problems in meetings
Telling the team about one person's illness

Reading staff's messages to learn how they feel

questions.stem: During a tense meeting, a manager sits with her arms crossed and frowns while staff speak. What message might staff take from this?
options: That she is closed to their views
That she agrees with every point
That she is fully relaxed and open

questions.stem: A manager uses her skill at reading people to pressure a junior officer into approving something against the rules. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since she achieved her goal
EI is being used to manipulate, not to help

questions.stem: Which item belongs in a manager's personal plan to develop her emotional intelligence?
options: A list of staff she wants to move out
A promise never to feel angry again
A target to avoid all difficult conversations
A goal, actions, support and review date

questions.stem: Which is a common warning sign of burnout in a staff member?
options: Taking normal breaks and annual leave
Asking questions in team meetings
Constant tiredness and cynicism
Sharing ideas for improving the work

questions.stem: A manager notices that one officer regularly works late to finish tasks that others have passed to him. What should she do?
options: Review the workload and share tasks fairly
Praise him for working longer than others

questions.stem: Before proposing a sensitive change at a statutory body, a manager finds out who has influence and how key people feel about it. Which EI skill is this?
options: Self-regulation
Social awareness

questions.stem: A manager is very upset after a heated meeting and must decide whether to discipline an officer. What is best?
options: Decide at once while the facts are fresh
Let the angriest person in the room decide
Ask the officer's friends what to do

questions.stem: In team meetings, two quiet officers rarely speak while others dominate. What should the manager do?
options: Assume the quiet officers have nothing to say
Criticise the officers who speak the most
Invite every member's view in turn

questions.stem: Which interview question best shows a candidate's emotional intelligence?
options: How did you handle a recent conflict?
What is your highest qualification?
How many years have you worked in government?
Which software packages can you use?

questions.stem: How can a manager keep improving her emotional intelligence over time?
options: Attend one workshop and then stop
Seek feedback and reflect regularly

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-letter short form is commonly used for emotional intelligence?
Give the surname of the writer who made emotional intelligence widely known in the 1990s with his five-part model.
What two-word term names the messages people send through posture, gestures and facial expression?
What two-word term, used by Goleman, names a sudden emotional reaction that overwhelms clear thinking?
What one-word term names a relationship of mutual understanding and trust between people?
Feedback gathered at the same time from a person's manager, peers and staff is called ___-degree feedback. What number fills the gap?
What one-word term names the practice of paying calm, full attention to the present moment, often used to manage stress?
What one-word term names feeling sorry for someone, as opposed to understanding their feelings from their point of view?
What one-word term names a situation or event that causes stress?
What one-word term describes stating your needs and views clearly and respectfully, without being passive or aggressive?
What two-word term names the effort of managing one's feelings to meet the demands of a job, such as staying calm with angry customers?
Which two-word model uses four "panes" to show what is known and unknown about yourself, to you and to others?
What two-word term names a team climate in which people feel safe to speak up, admit mistakes and try new ideas without fear?
In a feedback survey, five raters score a manager's listening as 3, 4, 2, 4 and 2 out of 5. What is her average score?
What one-word term names the ability to adjust calmly and quickly to new situations and changes?

essays.stem: Explain how a manager in a government agency can assess her own emotional strengths and weaknesses, and describe the personal development plan she should then prepare.
essays.modelAnswer: She can start with an honest self-assessment, using a recognised EI questionnaire and reflecting on recent situations: when she handled pressure well, and when she reacted in a way she regretted. A short reflective journal kept for a few weeks will show patterns, such as the situations that trigger irritation or anxiety. Because self-assessment can be biased, she should also ask for feedback from her manager, peers and staff, ideally through a confidential 360-degree process, and notice how people respond to her in meetings. Comparing these views with her own shows her blind spots. From this, she should choose two or three priorities, for example staying calm when challenged in meetings, or listening more before giving solutions. Her development plan would set a clear goal for each, the actions she will take, such as using a pause-and-breathe routine, practising summarising what others say, or attending a short course, the support she needs, such as a mentor or coach, and how she will know she has improved, for example better feedback scores. She would set review dates every three months and update the plan as she progresses.
markingPoints: Uses self-assessment and reflection, including a journal or questionnaire
Seeks feedback from others to check for blind spots
Chooses a small number of clear priorities
Plan sets goals, actions, support and measures of progress
Sets regular review dates and updates the plan

essays.stem: Describe how a manager's emotions and behaviour can affect the performance and wellbeing of a team, using examples from a public office.
essays.modelAnswer: Moods spread in a team, so a manager's emotions have a strong effect on everyone. If the manager at a tax office arrives tense and snaps at staff, they are likely to become anxious, avoid her and hide problems rather than ask for help, which leads to mistakes and slower service at the counter. Staff who feel criticised in public may lose confidence and stop suggesting improvements. Over time, a climate of fear can raise absence, stress-related illness and staff turnover, and members of the public may notice the tension in the way they are served. On the other hand, a manager who stays calm under pressure, explains decisions, listens and recognises good work helps staff feel safe and valued. They are then more willing to speak up about problems, help each other in busy periods and go the extra mile for the public. For example, during a backlog of applications, a manager who acknowledges the strain, shares a clear plan and works alongside the team is more likely to keep morale and quality up. The manager's behaviour therefore shapes the team's performance, wellbeing and the public's experience of the service.
markingPoints: Explains that a manager's emotions spread to the team
Gives examples of negative effects on performance and wellbeing
Gives examples of positive effects from calm, respectful behaviour
Links the effects to service to the public
Uses realistic examples from a public office

essays.stem: Evaluate the strategies a manager can use to manage her own emotions when under heavy pressure, such as during a crisis at a public hospital.
essays.modelAnswer: In the moment, short techniques are most useful. Pausing and taking a few slow breaths gives time to think before reacting, and naming the feeling, such as "I am frustrated", reduces its hold. These are quick and can be used anywhere, but on their own they do not remove the cause of the pressure. Reframing the situation, for example seeing a complaint as useful information rather than an attack, helps her respond constructively, although it takes practice to do well. Practical steps reduce pressure at its source: setting priorities, delegating, and asking for extra resources where the workload is unrealistic. These are among the most effective strategies, but depend on support from her own managers. Looking after her health through sleep, exercise and proper breaks builds resilience over time, although a crisis often makes this hard. Talking things through with a trusted colleague, mentor or the employee assistance programme helps her process strong feelings and avoid bottling them up. Suppressing emotions completely may seem professional but usually leads to stress and later outbursts. The best approach combines in-the-moment techniques with practical action and longer-term self-care, and she should seek professional help if stress persists.
markingPoints: Evaluates in-the-moment techniques such as pausing, breathing and naming feelings
Evaluates reframing and its limits
Evaluates practical steps to reduce the cause of pressure
Evaluates self-care and talking to others, and warns against suppression
Concludes with a balanced, combined approach and when to seek help

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can recognise the emotions of staff and members of the public accurately, and how she should avoid misreading them.
essays.modelAnswer: A manager can pick up emotions from what people say, how they say it and what their body shows. Words such as "fine" can carry very different meanings depending on tone, speed and volume. Facial expressions, eye contact, posture and gestures give further clues: crossed arms and a tight jaw may suggest anger or defensiveness, while a lowered head and quiet voice may suggest worry or sadness. Changes in normal behaviour are especially telling, such as a usually punctual officer arriving late, or a talkative person becoming withdrawn. Listening actively, by giving full attention, asking open questions and summarising what she heard, helps her understand the feelings behind the words. However, signals can easily be misread. Body language differs between people and cultures, someone may look stern simply because they are concentrating, and a manager's own mood can colour what she sees. To avoid mistakes, she should treat her reading as a guess to be checked, not a fact, for example by saying "You seem worried about this; is that right?" She should consider the context, avoid stereotypes, look at several signals together and respect a person's choice not to share their feelings.
markingPoints: Identifies verbal and tone cues
Identifies non-verbal cues and changes in normal behaviour
Uses active listening and open questions
Explains why signals can be misread, including culture and her own mood
Checks assumptions respectfully and respects privacy

essays.stem: A member of the public becomes angry and loud at the counter of a municipal corporation's revenue office. Describe how an officer should use emotional intelligence to handle the situation.
essays.modelAnswer: The officer should first manage her own reaction: notice her rising tension, take a breath and keep her voice calm and low, because responding with anger will make things worse. She should keep a safe distance. Next she should let the person speak without interrupting, show she is listening through eye contact and nods, and then acknowledge the feeling, for example "I can see you are frustrated after waiting so long." Acknowledging the feeling is not the same as agreeing with everything, but it often lowers the temperature. She should then ask open questions to find out the real problem, summarise it, and explain clearly what she can do and by when, without making promises she cannot keep. If the person needs a decision she cannot make, she should offer to involve her supervisor. Throughout, she should not take the anger personally, since it is usually about the situation. If the person becomes threatening or abusive, she should follow the office's procedure, call her supervisor or security, and put her own and others' safety first. Afterwards she should record the incident, talk it over with her supervisor if she is shaken, and note any lessons for the service.
markingPoints: Manages own emotions first and keeps calm and safe
Listens without interrupting and acknowledges the person's feelings
Finds the real problem and explains clearly what can be done
Involves a supervisor or security when needed and follows procedure
Records the incident and seeks support or lessons afterwards

essays.stem: Two senior officers in a ministry department have stopped speaking to each other after a disagreement, and the team is taking sides. Explain how you, as their manager, would use emotional intelligence to resolve the conflict.
essays.modelAnswer: I would act early, because the conflict is now affecting the whole team. First I would check my own feelings and any bias, so that I approach both officers fairly. I would meet each officer privately, ask open questions about what happened and how they feel, and listen without judging, summarising what I heard to show I understand. This often reveals the real issue, such as a feeling of being undermined or overlooked, rather than the task itself. I would acknowledge each person's feelings and remind them of the standards of conduct expected. Next, with their agreement, I would bring them together in a calm, private setting, set ground rules for respectful talk, and help each explain their view and listen to the other. I would steer the discussion towards shared goals and practical agreements, such as how work will be divided and how they will raise concerns in future. I would record the agreement and follow up after a few weeks. I would also speak to the team, without sharing private details, to stop the taking of sides. If the conflict continues or involves bullying, I would follow the formal grievance procedure with human resources.
markingPoints: Manages own bias and acts early and fairly
Listens privately to each person and acknowledges feelings
Brings them together with ground rules to focus on shared goals and agreements
Records and follows up, and addresses the wider team without breaching confidentiality
Uses the formal procedure if needed

essays.stem: Describe how a manager can promote the development of emotional intelligence in her team at a public agency.
essays.modelAnswer: The most powerful step is for the manager to model emotionally intelligent behaviour herself: staying calm under pressure, admitting her mistakes, listening before deciding and giving feedback respectfully. Staff learn more from what she does than from what she says. She can build psychological safety, so that people feel safe to raise concerns and admit errors without being blamed, for example by thanking staff who report problems. She can make time in team meetings to review difficult situations, such as a hard day at the service counter, asking what people felt, what helped and what they would do differently. Short training sessions or workshops on topics such as active listening, handling angry customers and managing stress give staff practical tools. She can coach individuals one-to-one, helping them to recognise their triggers and plan better responses, and encourage peer mentoring. Emotional intelligence can be included in performance conversations and development plans, so that it is valued alongside technical skills. She should recognise and praise examples of good emotional intelligence, such as calming a tense situation. Finally, she should make sure staff know about the employee assistance programme and support those who are struggling.
markingPoints: Models emotionally intelligent behaviour herself
Builds psychological safety and reviews difficult situations as a team
Provides training and one-to-one coaching
Includes EI in performance discussions and recognises good examples
Promotes wellbeing support such as the employee assistance programme

essays.stem: An officer who is normally reliable has become tearful, withdrawn and is making mistakes. Explain how her manager should respond, showing emotional intelligence while respecting appropriate boundaries.
essays.modelAnswer: The manager should not ignore the signs or begin with the mistakes. She should find a private, unhurried moment, say what she has noticed in a caring way, and ask how the officer is doing, for example "You don't seem yourself lately. Is everything all right?" She should listen without judging and accept that the officer may not want to share details. If the officer explains that she is struggling, the manager should show understanding and focus on what support can help at work, such as temporary changes to workload or hours, within the organisation's policies. She should make sure the officer knows about the employee assistance programme and encourage her to seek professional help, such as her doctor, especially if she mentions feeling hopeless. If there is any sign she may harm herself, the manager should get urgent help at once. The manager should respect boundaries: she is not a counsellor and should not probe for personal details. She must keep what is shared confidential, telling only those who need to know, such as human resources, with the officer's agreement. Once support is in place, she can address the mistakes fairly and agree a follow-up meeting.
markingPoints: Raises concern privately and caringly, without starting with the mistakes
Listens without judging and respects the officer's choice to share
Offers reasonable workplace support within policy
Refers to the EAP or professional help, and gets urgent help if there is risk of harm
Keeps boundaries and confidentiality, then follows up fairly

essays.stem: "For a manager in the public service, emotional intelligence matters more than technical knowledge." Evaluate this statement.
essays.modelAnswer: There is good support for the statement. Most management work is done through people: motivating staff, handling conflict, giving feedback, leading change and dealing with the public and politicians. A manager with high emotional intelligence builds trust, keeps the team calm under pressure and handles difficult conversations well, so staff perform better and stay longer. Many failures in management come not from lack of knowledge but from poor relationships, such as a brilliant officer who is promoted but cannot lead a team. Emotional intelligence also helps public servants respond fairly to people who are distressed or angry. However, the statement goes too far. A manager in a ministry must understand the laws, policies, budgets and procedures she is responsible for. Without that knowledge, she may make wrong or unlawful decisions however well she relates to people, and staff will lose respect for her judgement. Emotional intelligence can also be misused to manipulate people if it is not guided by integrity. On balance, both are needed: technical knowledge is the foundation for sound decisions, while emotional intelligence determines how well those decisions are made with and through people. The higher a manager rises, the more emotional intelligence matters.
markingPoints: Gives reasons supporting the importance of EI for managers
Uses examples, such as promotion failures or dealing with the public
Gives reasons why technical knowledge is still essential
Notes that EI can be misused without integrity
Reaches a balanced, justified conclusion

essays.stem: A statutory body is being restructured, and many staff fear for their jobs. Explain how a manager can use emotional intelligence to lead her team through the change.
essays.modelAnswer: The manager must first manage her own feelings, since she may be anxious too, and find support from her own manager or a mentor so that she can stay steady for her team. She should recognise that fear, anger and grief are normal reactions to change and that people move through them at different speeds. She should communicate early, honestly and often, sharing what is known, what is not yet known and when more information will come, rather than making promises she cannot keep. Rumours grow when there is silence. She should hold team meetings and one-to-one conversations, listen to concerns, acknowledge feelings and answer questions. She should watch for signs of stress, such as withdrawal or irritability, and make sure staff know about the employee assistance programme and any support for those who may be affected. Involving staff in shaping how the new structure will work gives them some control and uses their knowledge. She should keep the team focused on its service to the public, recognise their efforts during a hard time, and treat everyone fairly and consistently. Finally, she should mark progress and help the team settle into the new structure.
markingPoints: Manages her own emotions and seeks support
Recognises normal emotional reactions to change
Communicates honestly and often, without false promises
Listens, acknowledges feelings and supports wellbeing
Involves staff, keeps them focused, treats them fairly and recognises progress

practical1.title: Assess emotional intelligence and prepare development plans
practical1.brief: This task takes place in a made-up public body (for example a regional office of a ministry). First, as a group, prepare a poster that explains the main parts of emotional intelligence (self-awareness, self-management, motivation, empathy and social skills), with one realistic workplace example of each from the public service. Next, each member privately completes the EI self-assessment questionnaire provided by the assessor, then the group carries out a structured feedback exercise in pairs: each person gives their partner two strengths and one area to develop, using the feedback card and speaking respectfully. Finally, each member writes a one-page personal EI development plan with two goals, actions, support needed, measures of progress and review dates. Personal scores and plans are seen only by the member and the assessor. Give each member a named role for the group work: facilitator (keeps time and runs the feedback exercise fairly), poster designer, example researcher (prepares the public-service examples), feedback card keeper (makes sure every card is completed and handed to its owner), and reviewer (checks the poster for accuracy). In a group of four, the facilitator also reviews the poster. Every member completes their own questionnaire and plan.
materials: EI self-assessment questionnaires and feedback cards from the assessor
Poster paper, markers and sticky notes
photos: The group's plan showing roles and timings
The finished poster with the five parts of EI and examples
The feedback exercise in progress (hands and cards only, no faces unless all agree)
Completed feedback cards, photographed with names covered
A completed development plan template, photographed with personal details covered
checklist: Took a named role and contributed to the poster
Poster explains each part of EI accurately with a realistic example
Completed the self-assessment honestly and reflected on the result
Gave feedback that was specific, balanced and respectful
Received feedback calmly and asked questions to understand it
Development plan has clear goals, actions, support, measures and review dates
Kept other members' scores and feedback confidential
safety: Personal scores, feedback and plans are confidential: share only with the assessor and do not photograph names
Speak respectfully; feedback is about behaviour, not personality
Any member may pass on discussing a personal example, without explanation
If the activity raises distress for anyone, pause and speak to the assessor, who can refer to support services

practical2.title: Use emotional intelligence in workplace role plays and write a counter guide
practical2.brief: Your group works in a made-up public service office (for example a tax office or a passport office). The assessor gives you three short scenario cards: an angry member of the public at the counter, a manager giving difficult feedback to an upset officer, and two colleagues in conflict over a shared task. Plan and act out each role play for about eight minutes. In each, two members take the main roles and the others observe, using an EI observation checklist to note what helped and what did not (calm voice, acknowledging feelings, active listening, open questions, clear next steps). After each role play, hold a short debrief led by one member. Rotate so that every member takes a main role at least once and observes at least once. Finally, as a group, write a one-page guide for officers on using emotional intelligence at the service counter, based on what you learned. Give each member a named role for the planning and writing: scenario planner (prepares the role cards and timings), debrief leader, checklist keeper (collects and summarises the observation sheets), guide writer, and editor (checks the guide is accurate and clear). In a group of four, the checklist keeper also edits the guide. Photograph each stage and hand in the observation sheets, debrief notes and guide.
materials: Scenario cards and EI observation checklists from the assessor
A table and chairs set up as a service counter
Computer and printer for the guide (optional)
photos: The plan showing who plays and who observes in each role play
The service counter set-up for the first role play
A role play in progress (photographed from behind or of hands and notes if anyone prefers no face)
The debrief notes on the flipchart
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
In a main role, stayed calm and managed their own reactions
Acknowledged the other person's feelings and listened actively
Reached a clear, fair next step in the role play
As an observer, recorded specific, useful notes
Gave and received debrief feedback respectfully
Guide is accurate, practical and in plain language
safety: Keep role plays realistic but controlled: no physical contact, no shouting directly into anyone's face, and stop at once if the assessor or a player says "pause"
Use made-up names and situations, never real colleagues or members of the public
Feedback is about behaviour in the role play, not about the person
Anyone who finds a scenario upsetting may swap roles or step out, and can speak to the assessor afterwards
